title: Scamming is now bigger than narcotics trade
full_text:
Intelligence agencies calculate the international scam economy is now bigger than the illegal narcotics trade and is being run by sophisticated offshore networks using artificial intelligence that has supercharged their ability to dupe victims and hide their tracks.
White-collar crime and money-laundering agencies from across the Pacific signed a new intelligence sharing deal with Nauru on Wednesday at a gathering in Sydney of the Pacific Financial Intelligence Community, where the proliferation of scamming and cybercrime were discussed.
Brendan Thomas, chief executive of Australia's financial crimes regulator AUSTRAC, said criminal networks are spreading throughout the Pacific using sophisticated "scam compounds" as well as money laundering ventures targeting island nations and funnelling money between Australia, South America and the Middle East.
Thomas said scam networks cost the global economy more money than the narcotics trade and were rapidly increasing their activities in new regions due to AI. In Australia, the ACCC estimates financial scams alone cost individuals caught up in them a combined total of more than $2 billion per year.
"The technology is allowing, particularly the scammers to do things faster and at a greater scale than they've been able to do in the past," Thomas said.
"Those global scam centres hadn't been tackling the Pacific countries to the extent they've been concentrating on other parts of the world but now we're seeing it spread throughout the Pacific."
Traditional scams such as investment scams, social media phishing and business email compromise were being executed on a greater scale than previously due to AI, he said.
"People are also talking about the link between broader diasporas of Pacific communities in other parts of the world and scams happening in the Pacific. There certainly seems to be a link of that kind both in terms of the movement of money but hopefully in the prevention of those kinds of scam activities as well."
Supervisor of the Nauru Financial Intelligence Unit and PFIC co-chair Rajas Swarmy said sophisticated financial crime activity across the Pacific had increased significantly with white-collar crime recruiting local "money mules" in the region to traffic the proceeds of the drug trade.
"That particular mule would collect funds from others and then move it across the jurisdiction and out of the area," Swarmy said.
The rapid increase in financial crimes in the Pacific has heightened the need for information sharing among nations. Australia has already had successes tracing illicit funds to South American and Middle Eastern nations through existing information sharing schemes with Pacific nations.
"Most countries can trace funds to our border ... but the multilateral intelligence projects have meant analysts from multiple countries coming together, putting all their data on the table and then building a collective picture of the flow of money," Thomas said.
